speaker: Jigar Shah
title: Jigar Shah on the DOE's Role In Accelerating The Energy Transition
question: In electric utility grids, why does upgrading local distribution circuits to handle electric vehicle charging peaks drive up per-kilowatt-hour delivery costs so sharply?
guest: The utility company's coming in and saying, 'Well, we're going to spend $70 million to redo the distribution grid.' It's a lot cheaper for the utility just to put in a $1,000 bidirectional charger in my garage and say, 'When everyone's plugged in at the same time, we're going to ramp everybody down from 10 kilowatts of draw to only one kilowatt of draw so that we don't have to upgrade this entire distribution circuit.' Most of the time my distribution circuit here on my block has an average capacity factor of maybe 30%, which means it's only being used roughly 30% of the time. They're going to spend $75 million to expand that and drop utilization down to 15% just because a bunch of people bought electric vehicles. At some point, that math doesn't work. We've doubled the cost of transmission and distribution infrastructure in our country—from roughly two cents a kilowatt-hour to roughly four cents—largely because we keep overbuilding it and using it less and less on an average basis. If you want to use it more, you fluctuate flexible loads like EV chargers or use your house as thermal storage.

points.core: Local distribution circuits already sit idle for most hours of the day.
points.note: Accept: low baseline grid utilization or capacity factors (e.g., ~30-50%) on neighborhood wires outside brief peak windows. Do not credit: generic claims that the grid is old or crumbling.

points.core: Overbuilding fixed grid capacity for rare peaks lowers average asset utilization further.
points.note: Accept: expanding wires for simultaneous peak charging reduces capacity factor (e.g., from ~30% to ~15%), spreading higher fixed capital costs over fewer utilized hours and inflating per-kWh delivery rates. Do not credit: generic complaints about inflation or construction costs.

points.core: Throttling flexible loads during peaks avoids costly physical upgrades to distribution circuits.
points.note: Accept: managed EV charging (ramping draw down when everyone plugs in) or pre-cooling homes as thermal storage to smooth peaks at a fraction of grid-rebuild cost. Do not credit: generic advice to use less electricity overall.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core reason is that distribution equipment is sized for peak demand, but its cost is recovered over total energy delivered. Transformers, feeders, and substations must be rated for the highest coincident load they will ever see, even if that peak lasts only a few hours a day. When EV drivers plug in at the same time, typically early evening on top of the existing residential peak, they raise the peak far more than they raise average throughput. The utility then has to replace transformers, reconductor lines, and expand substations to serve capacity that sits idle most of the time.

Because these are large, lumpy, long-lived capital investments recovered through rates (plus an allowed return), a low load factor means the fixed cost is spread over relatively few additional kilowatt-hours, so the cost per kWh climbs steeply. Clustering makes it worse: a few Level 2 chargers on one street can overload a single neighborhood transformer.

The premise is conditional, though. If charging is shifted off-peak through time-of-use rates or managed charging, EVs add sales using existing capacity, which can actually lower per-kWh delivery costs.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Local distribution infrastructure—such as neighborhood transformers, underground cables, and substation feeders—must be sized for peak power demand (kilowatts) rather than total energy delivered (kilowatt-hours). When multiple electric vehicles on the same circuit plug in simultaneously during evening peak hours, they create sharp, coincident demand spikes that can overload local equipment for a few hours while leaving those same wires lightly used the rest of the day. 

Accommodating these brief spikes requires lumpy, capital-intensive upgrades—such as trenching pavement, reconductoring lines, and installing larger transformers—built in discrete capacity jumps that far exceed immediate average demand. Under utility rate regulation, utilities recover these steep fixed capital outlays, plus financing costs and a regulated return on equity, primarily through volumetric charges on total kilowatt-hours sold. Because unmanaged EV charging expands peak capacity requirements much faster than it adds round-the-clock energy sales, the circuit's load factor drops. Spreading massive, upfront construction and hardware costs across a relatively modest volume of incremental kilowatt-hours drives per-kilowatt-hour delivery costs sharply higher.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The premise is only partly right. Distribution upgrades can raise delivery costs, but the evidence so far doesn't show EVs driving per-kWh costs up sharply. Several studies, including Synapse Energy Economics' analysis of California and New York, found that EV customers paid more in utility revenue than the costs they added, which put slight downward pressure on rates.

The real problem is that distribution costs depend on peak demand, not energy. Transformers, feeders and service drops have to be sized for the highest simultaneous load, measured in kilowatts. If several homes on one transformer start Level 2 chargers at 6 p.m., on top of the evening peak, that equipment may need replacing even though total energy use rises only modestly. Those upgrades are expensive, lumpy and long-lived, and they serve a peak that may last only a few hours a year. When their cost is recovered through volumetric rates, every kilowatt-hour pays for that rarely used capacity.

Upgrades raise per-kWh costs mainly when charging is unmanaged and lines up with the existing peak. Time-of-use rates, managed or smart charging, and overnight charging use spare capacity instead. Those added kilowatt-hours spread fixed costs over more sales and can lower rates.

models.answer: Local distribution equipment—such as neighborhood transformers, feeders, and substations—must be sized for peak instantaneous power demand (kilowatts) rather than average energy use (kilowatt-hours). Electric vehicle charging, especially when drivers plug in simultaneously after work or use high-power fast chargers, creates sharp, brief demand spikes on circuits that sit lightly loaded most of the day. Because a local circuit serves relatively few customers, it lacks the load diversity that smooths out fluctuations at the broader transmission level, so coincident charging peaks easily exceed existing capacity. Upgrading that infrastructure requires large, lumpy fixed capital investments—such as replacing transformers, reconductoring lines, or trenching underground cables—that utilities recover through rates alongside financing and maintenance costs. When those heavy fixed expenses are spread over the relatively modest volume of extra kilowatt-hours delivered during short charging peaks, the resulting low asset utilization (or load factor) pushes the per-kilowatt-hour delivery cost sharply upward.

Utilities size local transformers and distribution lines for the highest load they must carry at any one time. If many EVs plug in when household demand is already high, even a short surge can push a neighborhood circuit past its capacity. The utility may have to replace a transformer or upgrade an entire stretch of line, taking on costs it must recover year-round even if the extra capacity is needed only a few hours at a time.

Delivery costs rise sharply per kilowatt-hour when those upgrades add more to annual costs, in percentage terms, than EV charging adds to annual electricity sales. Spreading charging across off-peak hours can deliver the same amount of energy using spare capacity, often deferring the upgrade.
